meta.title: The Classical World
meta.subtitle: From the Persian Wars to the rise of Islam: Europe, Africa, the Near East, Asia and the Americas, c. 500 BCE – 650 CE
meta.description: Empires and cultures of the classical and late antique world, from the Persian Wars and Warring States China to the fall of the Sasanians and the founding of Tang. It overlaps Ancient Civilizations from 500 to 330 BCE.
meta.credits: Dates and events come from English Wikipedia (read 17 November 2026) and the scholarly works it cites; each event lists its sources. Ancient dates are uncertain and scholars disagree. The lighter parts of a bar show the range of dates the cited sources give for its start and end, and the Dating menu re-plots a region under another dating system. Compiled with AI assistance and not yet reviewed by a specialist.

events.title: Alexander the Great takes Tyre
events.descr: After a siege during which he builds a causeway to the island city. Eight thousand Tyrians die and 30,000 are sold into slavery.

events.title: Greco-Persian Wars
events.descr: From the Ionian Revolt to the end of hostilities; Persian invasions of Greece are repulsed in 492–490 and 480–479 BCE.

events.title: Alexander conquers the Achaemenid Empire
events.descr: The end of a Macedonian campaign that began in 336 BCE.

events.title: Warring States period
events.descr: Qin deposes the last Zhou king in 256 BCE and unifies China in 221 BCE.

events.title: La Venta Great Pyramid
events.descr: A radiocarbon date from Complex C, the great pyramid.

events.title: Earliest Maya writing
events.descr: The earliest inscriptions in an identifiably Maya script, in the Petén Basin.

events.title: Gauls defeat Rome at the Allia and sack the city
events.descr: Celts under Brennus defeat the Romans and sack Rome. The traditional (Varronian) date is 390 BCE; modern historians consider c. 387 the most probable.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox and Date of the battle

source.sourceLocation: Date of the battle (Polybius; most probable)

events.title: Latin League dissolved
events.descr: The league of Latin cities is dissolved.

events.title: Battle of Marathon
events.descr: The Persians are defeated in their first invasion of Greece.

events.title: Battle of Salamis
events.descr: A naval battle during Xerxes' invasion of Greece (481–479 BCE).

events.title: Peloponnesian War
events.descr: Athens and Sparta fight for hegemony over Greece; Persia backs Sparta from 413 and Athens surrenders in 404.

events.title: Reign of Philip II of Macedon
events.descr: King of Macedon from 359 BCE. He is assassinated in 336 and immediately succeeded by his son Alexander.

events.title: Philip II wins the Battle of Chaeronea
events.descr: The next year (337 BCE) Philip becomes hegemon of the Hellenic League.

events.title: Macedon moves its capital from Aigai to Pella
events.descr: Pella remains the capital until the kingdom ends in 168 BCE.

events.title: Samnite Wars
events.descr: Three wars (343–341, 327–304, 298–290 BCE) in which Rome subjugates the Samnites, despite their great victory at the Caudine Forks (321).

events.title: Teres I founds the Odrysian kingdom
events.descr: A Thracian kingdom founded after the failed Persian invasion of Greece. Philip II of Macedon conquers it in 340 BCE; Seuthes III revives it around 330.

events.title: Battle of Himera
events.descr: The Greeks of Sicily defeat Hamilcar's expedition, crippling Carthage's power on the island for decades. Tradition put it on the same day as Salamis; modern scholars reject that.

events.title: Athenian expedition to Sicily
events.descr: Athens attacks Syracuse during the Peloponnesian War; the expedition is destroyed in 413 BCE.

events.title: Philip II defeats Ateas
events.descr: The Scythian king Ateas is killed in battle against Philip II of Macedon in Dobruja, and his empire falls to pieces.

events.title: Pazyryk burials
events.descr: Burials at Pazyryk and neighbouring sites in the Altai. A Saka (eastern Scythian) culture.

source.sourceLocation: Archaeology ('5th century BC'): start of century

events.title: Bantu speakers reach Lake Victoria and Angola
events.descr: The Western Stream reaches the southern edge of the rainforest and central Angola; the Eastern Stream, with Urewe pottery and one of the oldest iron-smelting centres in Africa, reaches west of Lake Victoria.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Western Stream and Eastern Stream

events.title: Herodotus describes the Garamantes
events.descr: The earliest written record of them: "a very great nation" who herded cattle and farmed dates.

source.sourceLocation: History ('5th century BC'): start of century

events.title: Life of the Buddha
events.descr: He lives under Bimbisara and dies under Ajatashatru. Most scholars who give a date place his death within 20 years of 400 BCE; earlier scholarship used 563–483 BCE.

source.sourceLocation: infobox and Dating ('the earlier dates of 563–483 BCE')
infobox and Dating ('within 20 years either side of 400 BCE')

events.title: The Nanda dynasty takes Magadha
events.descr: The Nandas usurp the Shishunaga throne; Chandragupta Maurya overthrows them.

events.title: Sa Huỳnh–Kalanay trade network
events.descr: A trade sphere reaching Taiwan, southern Thailand, Borneo and the Philippines. The Sa Huỳnh, who buried their cremated dead in lidded jars, were most likely predecessors of the Austronesian-speaking Cham.

events.title: Metal tools in the Philippines
events.descr: Metal tools appear somewhere around 500 BC (Jocano: between 500 BC and 1 AD); other evidence points to iron in the ninth and tenth centuries BC.

source.sourceLocation: iron 'during the ninth and tenth centuries B.C.'

events.title: Kalanay Cave pottery
events.descr: Pottery dated 400 BC to AD 1500, similar to that of the Sa Huỳnh culture of southern Vietnam; iron and bronze artifacts were found at the site. It names the Sa Huỳnh–Kalanay interaction sphere, an Iron Age maritime trading network associated with the Austronesian peoples.

events.title: Buni culture in northern West Java
events.descr: A clay pottery culture on the coast of northern West Java, Jakarta and Banten, known for incised geometric decoration; burial gifts date from 400 BC to AD 100. The kingdom of Tarumanagara is probably its successor.

events.title: The kingdom of Lihyan at Dadan
events.descr: Most likely founded after Nabonidus arrived in north-west Arabia; it flourished for at least a century and a half. F. Winnett’s longer chronology places its beginning in the 6th century BC. The Gulf of Aqaba was called the Gulf of Lihyan.

events.title: Alexander the Great attacks the Getae
events.descr: On the lower Danube. Herodotus first used the name Getae; the Dacians were influenced by the Scythians and by the La Tène Celts who arrived in the 4th century BC.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Name and Origins and ethnogenesis

events.title: Adena burial mounds
events.descr: Mounds built from hundreds of thousands of baskets of graded earth serve as burial and ceremonial sites; trade runs from Great Lakes copper to Gulf Coast shells. The Great Serpent Mound has been attributed to the culture, without conclusive evidence.

events.title: The Dorset culture begins
events.descr: They hunt seals from holes in the ice and make soapstone lamps (qulliq) burning seal oil; unlike earlier cultures they lack bow and arrow.

events.title: Monte Albán founded
events.descr: Built on a mountaintop in a previously uninhabited no-man’s-land; about 5,200 people live there by around 300 BCE. The Danzantes carvings date from its earliest period and show traits of Olmec culture.

events.title: Saladoid potters reach the Lesser Antilles and Puerto Rico
events.descr: Farmers and potters living in settled villages, believed to have spoken an Arawakan language; they displace the pre-ceramic Ortoiroid culture.

events.title: Nyatri Tsenpo, first Yarlung king (traditional date)
events.descr: Some Tibetan texts give 126 BC, others 414 BC. Tibetan texts name the kingdom of Zhangzhung (c. 500 BC–625 AD) as the precursor of later Tibetan kingdoms.

events.title: Battle of Thermopylae
events.descr: Greek city-states led by Sparta under Leonidas I hold the pass against Xerxes’ invasion; the Greeks defeat the invaders at Salamis later that year.

events.title: Pericles leads Athens
events.descr: The statesman and general of the Golden Age of Athens dies of the Plague of Athens in 429 BC.

events.title: The Parthenon built
events.descr: A temple on the Athenian Acropolis dedicated to Athena, begun when the Delian League was at the peak of its power; work on its decoration continued until 432 BC.

events.title: The trial and death of Socrates
events.descr: Athens tries the 70-year-old philosopher on two charges and he is put to death.

events.title: Plato founds the Academy
events.descr: Aristotle studies there for twenty years (367–347 BC); the school lasts until 83 BC.

events.title: Aristotle founds the Lyceum
events.descr: Returning to Athens after it fell under Macedonian rule, Aristotle sets up his school at the Lyceum.

events.title: The Mausoleum at Halicarnassus
events.descr: The tomb of Mausolus, built after his death in 353 BC; one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

events.title: Herodotus, historian of the Greco-Persian Wars
events.descr: A Greek historian and geographer from Halicarnassus; nothing in his Histories can be dated with certainty after 430 BC.

events.title: Mozi founds Mohism
events.descr: A philosophy emphasising universal love, social order, the will of Heaven, sharing and honouring the worthy.

events.title: The Hundred Schools of Thought
events.descr: Confucianism, Taoism, Mohism, Legalism and others flourish in the late Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods; their ideas profoundly influence East Asian culture.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Confucianism, Taoism, Mohism and Legalism

events.title: Shang Yang’s reforms in Qin
events.descr: The reformer takes office in Qin in 359 BCE; his first reforms (356 BC) assign land by military merit and favour agriculture, and a second set follows in 350 BC.

events.title: Pāṇini’s Sanskrit grammar
events.descr: The ancient Sanskrit grammarian flourished in the mid 1st millennium BCE, variously dated between the 6th–5th and the 4th century BCE.

events.title: Death of Alexander the Great
events.descr: He dies at the age of 32, between the evenings of 10 and 11 June 323 BCE; fighting between his generals starts almost immediately.

events.title: Wars of the Diadochi
events.descr: Conflicts between Alexander’s generals over his empire. Ptolemy receives Egypt; after Corupedium (281 BC) Seleucus I is the last of the original successors, and Macedon is settled for the Antigonids only in 272 BC with the death of Pyrrhus.

events.title: Battle of Ipsus
events.descr: A coalition of Seleucus, Cassander and Lysimachus defeats Antigonus I, who is killed.

events.title: Seleucus takes Babylon: the Seleucid Empire
events.descr: After the battle of Gaza (312 BC), Seleucus captures the citadel of Babylon in August 311 BC. His empire is annexed by Rome under Pompey in 63 BC.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, infobox, Rise of Seleucus and Babylonian War

events.title: Ptolemy I becomes pharaoh: the Ptolemaic Kingdom
events.descr: Ptolemy, who had ruled Egypt as satrap since 323 BC, takes the title of basileus and pharaoh. The kingdom lasts until the death of Cleopatra VII in 30 BC.

events.title: The Library of Alexandria
events.descr: Probably built under Ptolemy II Philadelphus (285–246 BC), though Ptolemy I may have planned it. Its decline begins with a purge of intellectuals in 145 BC; part is burned by Julius Caesar in 48 BC.

events.title: The Greco-Bactrian Kingdom breaks away
events.descr: Founded by the Seleucid satrap Diodotus I; it falls around 120 BC as the Parthians and nomads such as the Saka and Yuezhi press in. The Yuezhi later found the Kushan Empire.

events.title: Archimedes killed at the siege of Syracuse
events.descr: One of the greatest mathematicians of all time (c. 287 – c. 212 BC), he designed war machines to defend Syracuse and was killed by a Roman soldier.

events.title: The Rosetta Stone decree
events.descr: A decree issued at Memphis on behalf of Ptolemy V Epiphanes on 27 March 196 BC.

events.title: Battle of Pydna: Rome ends the Antigonid kingdom
events.descr: Defeat in the Third Macedonian War ends the dynasty that had ruled much of Hellenistic Greece since 294 BC.

events.title: Attalus III leaves Pergamon to Rome
events.descr: The childless king bequeaths his realm to the Roman Republic; after a revolt it becomes the Roman province of Asia (129 BC).

events.title: First Punic War
events.descr: It breaks out on Sicily and lasts twenty-three years, until Carthage is defeated.

events.title: Second Punic War: Hannibal
events.descr: Hannibal is defeated at Zama in 202 BC and a treaty follows in 201 BC.

events.title: Rome destroys Carthage
events.descr: Rome declares war in 149 BC and storms Carthage in 146 BC; its territory becomes the Roman province of Africa.

events.title: Battle of Carrhae: Parthia defeats Crassus
events.descr: Fought between the Roman Republic and the Parthian Empire; Cicero called the war "nulla causa", since Parthia had a treaty with Rome.

events.title: Julius Caesar assassinated
events.descr: Killed on the Ides of March (15 March), three days before he was to leave on a campaign against the Parthians; the Liberators’ civil war follows (43–42 BC).

events.title: Battle of Actium
events.descr: On 2 September 31 BC Octavian’s fleet under Agrippa defeats Antony and Cleopatra. Cleopatra takes her life on 12 August 30 BC, ending the Ptolemaic Kingdom and the Hellenistic period, and Egypt becomes a Roman province.

events.title: Octavian becomes Augustus: the Roman Empire
events.descr: The Senate grants Octavian the title Augustus on 16 January 27 BC, often seen as the end of the Republic. He rules as the first emperor until his death in AD 14 and makes peace with Parthia and Kush.

events.title: The Roman Empire at its greatest extent
events.descr: At the time of Trajan’s death (r. 98–117 AD) the empire covers some 5,000,000 km².

events.title: Crisis of the Third Century
events.descr: It begins with the assassination of Severus Alexander by his own troops; by 268 the empire has split into three competing states, and Aurelian (270–275) turns the tide.

events.title: The Tetrarchy
events.descr: Diocletian divides imperial rule between two augusti and two caesares; Constantine’s victory at the Milvian Bridge (312) begins its end.

events.title: Edict of Milan
events.descr: The 13 February 313 agreement to treat Christians benevolently; Christianity becomes the state religion with the Edict of Thessalonica in 380.

events.title: Constantinople becomes the capital
events.descr: Founded in 324 on the site of Byzantium and dedicated on 11 May 330 as the new eastern capital of the Roman Empire.

events.title: Battle of Adrianople
events.descr: In 376 the Huns had driven many Goths into the empire; at Adrianople they defeat the Romans.

events.title: Death of Theodosius I: East and West divide
events.descr: He dies after making Christianity the state religion, ending the unified empire (27 BC – AD 395).

sources.sourceLocation: infobox and Transition to late antiquity

events.title: The Visigoths sack Rome
events.descr: On 24 August 410 Alaric’s Visigoths enter Rome and pillage it for three days. The Vandals sack it again in 455.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Third siege and sack, and Aftermath

events.title: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
events.descr: Odoacer deposes Romulus Augustulus, the last Western emperor, and sends the imperial insignia to the Eastern emperor Zeno.

sources.sourceLocation: lead and Fall in the West

events.title: Reign of Justinian I
events.descr: He rewrites Roman law as the Corpus Juris Civilis (final code 534) and retakes North Africa from the Vandals (533–534) and Italy from the Ostrogoths; the empire reaches its zenith in 555.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, Life, Legislative activities, Conquest of North Africa, War in Italy and Results

events.title: Hagia Sophia built
events.descr: Justinian’s basilica rises after the second church burns in the Nika riots of January 532; it is inaugurated on 27 December 537.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, infobox and Church of Justinian I

events.title: The Plague of Justinian
events.descr: It reaches Roman Egypt in 541 and every corner of the empire by 543; Justinian catches it and recovers. It strikes the Sasanian Empire too and recurs until the mid-8th century.

events.title: The Parthian Empire
events.descr: Centred in ancient Iran; Mithridates I (r. c. 171–132 BC) greatly expands it by seizing Media and Mesopotamia from the Seleucids.

events.title: The Maccabean Revolt
events.descr: A revolt against the Seleucid king Antiochus IV’s repression of Judaism. The Maccabees take Jerusalem in 164 BCE; Judas Maccabeus dies in 160, and in 141 Simon Thassi expels the Greeks. An alliance with Rome helps secure independence.

events.title: Herod the Great rules Judea
events.descr: A Roman client king; after his death the Romans divide his kingdom among his heirs. Some scholars (Steinmann) date his reign 36–1 BCE.

events.title: Crucifixion of Jesus
events.descr: In Jerusalem, in the Roman province of Judaea; dated AD 30 or 33.

events.title: Rome destroys Jerusalem and the Second Temple
events.descr: The decisive event of the First Jewish Revolt (66–73 CE): the siege runs from 13 April to 8 September 70.

events.title: The Bar Kokhba revolt
events.descr: Sparked by Hadrian’s plan to rebuild Jerusalem as Aelia Capitolina; the rebels hold an independent state for over three years until Betar falls in 135. The province is renamed Syria Palaestina.

events.title: Rome annexes the Nabataean Kingdom
events.descr: Independent since the mid-3rd century BC, it becomes the province of Arabia Petraea.

events.title: The Sasanian Empire
events.descr: Ardashir I defeats the Parthians at the Battle of Hormozdgan on 28 April 224; the last pre-Islamic Iranian empire rules from Ctesiphon until 651.

events.title: Shapur I defeats Rome at Edessa
events.descr: A disastrous Roman defeat; the same year Odaenathus of Palmyra defeats Shapur near the Euphrates.

events.title: Zenobia’s Palmyrene Empire
events.descr: In 270 Zenobia rapidly conquers most of the Roman east, including Egypt; in 271 she claims the imperial title. Aurelian besieges Palmyra in 272 and razes it after a revolt in 273.

events.title: Armenia adopts Christianity
events.descr: The traditional date; scholars propose dates from 284 to no later than 325, and many favour 314.

events.title: Aksum conquers Himyar
events.descr: After the conquest Christianity becomes Himyar’s main religion; Sasanian intervention brings Yemen under Persian influence in 575 or 578.

events.title: The last Roman–Persian war
events.descr: The Sasanians conquer much of the Levant, parts of Anatolia and, for the first time, Egypt; they take Jerusalem after a three-week siege in 614. Heraclius strikes back from 622, the Persians fail before Constantinople in 626, and Persia, torn by civil war, seeks peace.

events.title: The Hijrah: start of the Islamic calendar
events.descr: Its date equates to 16 July 622; the year is the epoch of the Islamic calendar.

events.title: Battle of the Yarmuk
events.descr: On 15–20 August 636 the Rashidun Caliphate defeats the Byzantine army; Byzantine Syria is annexed.

events.title: Battle of al-Qadisiyyah
events.descr: The second Rashidun invasion of Sasanian territory wins a decisive victory (16–19 November 636).

events.title: Fall of the Sasanian Empire
events.descr: By 651 most cities of the Iranian lands are in Muslim hands; the Rashidun Caliphate annexes the empire.

events.title: Chandragupta Maurya founds the Maurya Empire
events.descr: His conquest of Magadha is generally dated to c. 322–319 BCE; an alternative chronology places these events in c. 311–305 BCE. He reigns until c. 297 BCE.

events.title: Seleucid–Mauryan war
events.descr: Fought sometime between 305 and 303 BCE between Chandragupta and Seleucus I Nicator; it ends in a marriage alliance.

events.title: Reign of Ashoka
events.descr: Mauryan emperor from c. 268 BCE until his death in 232 BCE. His edicts, inscriptions of the 3rd century BCE, are read again only after the decipherment of the Brahmi script in the 19th century.

events.title: Kalinga War
events.descr: Ashoka conquers Kalinga in the eighth year of his reign, according to his own edicts. The war began an era of more than 40 years of relative peace.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, Course of the war and Aftermath

source.sourceLocation: infobox and Course of the war

events.title: Buddhism reaches Sri Lanka
events.descr: Theravada Buddhism is introduced during the reign of King Devanampiya Tissa.

events.title: Pushyamitra Shunga kills the last Maurya
events.descr: The assassination of Brihadratha by Pushyamitra Shunga ends the Maurya Empire and begins the Shunga Empire.

events.title: Demetrius I invades India: the Indo-Greek Kingdom
events.descr: The Graeco-Bactrian king Demetrius I invades India from Bactria. The Indo-Greeks disappear as a political entity around 10 AD.

events.title: Menander I
events.descr: Indo-Greek king; the precise dates of his reign remain elusive. Patanjali’s Mahabhashya, around 150 BC, describes a failed campaign of Menander as far as Mathura. According to tradition, he embraced the Buddhist faith.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Reign and Menander and Buddhism

events.title: Maues, the first Saka king in India
events.descr: The first rulers of the Indo-Scythian kingdom are Maues (c. 85–60 BCE) and Vonones (c. 75–65 BCE).

events.title: Kujula Kadphises unites the Yuezhi: the Kushan Empire
events.descr: Kujula Kadphises (25–85), the first ruler, unites the Yuezhi tribes into a confederation. The Kushan Empire fragments into semi-independent kingdoms in the 3rd century AD.

events.title: A Kushan army fights Ban Chao near Khotan
events.descr: Ban Chao fights battles near Khotan with a Kushan army of 70,000 men.

sources.sourceLocation: Conquests in India and Central Asia

events.title: Reign of Kanishka
events.descr: The empire reaches its zenith. Around 127 CE he replaces Greek with Bactrian as the official language of administration. He never converts to Buddhism but gives it royal sponsorship, and heads the 4th Buddhist Council in Kashmir. Earlier scholars dated his accession to 78 CE.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, infobox and Kanishka and Buddhism

events.title: Naneghat inscription of Satakarni I
events.descr: Dated to 70–60 BCE, in the reign of Satakarni I.

events.title: The Pallavas become a major southern power
events.descr: During the reigns of Mahendravarman I (600–630) and Narasimhavarman I (630–668).

events.title: Kashyapa I rules from Sigiriya
events.descr: Kashyapa I (473–491) chooses Sigiriya to be his capital.

events.title: Coronation of Chandragupta I
events.descr: Crowned on 26 February 320. The Gupta Empire, established c. 240, exists from the mid 3rd century to the mid 6th century CE.

events.title: Reign of Samudragupta
events.descr: The second Gupta emperor. Modern scholars variously assign the start of his reign from c. 319 CE to c. 350 CE.

events.title: Reign of Chandragupta II
events.descr: Gupta emperor until his death in c. 415. The beginning of his reign can be dated to either 376–377 CE or 380–381 CE.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, infobox and Period of reign

events.title: Chandragupta II defeats the last Western Satrap
events.descr: Rudrasimha III, the last of the Western Satraps, is defeated by the Gupta emperor Chandragupta II.

events.title: Nalanda founded
events.descr: Established by the Gupta emperor Kumaragupta I; it operates for almost a thousand years, until around 1400 CE.

events.title: Gupta–Hunnic Wars
events.descr: Wars between the Gupta Empire and the Huns; the Alchon Huns invade India between the 4th and 6th centuries CE.

events.title: Ajanta Caves: the second phase
events.descr: Buddhist cave monuments dating from the second century BCE to about 480 CE. The second phase falls in a brief period of 460–480 CE according to later scholarship (400–650 CE in older accounts), circa 480 CE under King Harishena.

events.title: Aryabhata
events.descr: Mathematician-astronomer of the Gupta era. He states he was 23 years old in 3600 Kali Yuga, 499 CE. His Aryabhatiya is translated into Arabic c. 820 CE.

events.title: Harsha, emperor of Kannauj
events.descr: Crowned at an assembly in April 606, after the downfall of the Gupta Empire in the middle of the 6th century; he rules until his death in 647. An invasion he leads is repelled on the banks of the Narmada in the winter of 618–619.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, infobox, Early years and Reign

events.title: Tang Taizong sends Wang Xuance to India
events.descr: The Tang Chinese emperor Tang Taizong sends Wang Xuance to India.

events.title: Qin unifies China
events.descr: Beginning in 230 BC, the Qin under King Ying Zheng wage a series of wars; by 221 BC he has conquered all the other warring states, ending the Warring States period, and rules as Qin Shi Huang.

events.title: Qin Shi Huang dies; the Terracotta Army
events.descr: Qin Shi Huang dies on 12 July 210 BC, during his fifth tour of eastern China. Work on his mausoleum began in 246 BCE; the Terracotta Army was buried with him in 210–209 BCE and discovered by farmers on 29 March 1974.

events.title: Liu Bang proclaimed emperor: the Han dynasty
events.descr: The Qin surrender to Liu Bang in 207 BC and Xianyang is destroyed in 206 BC. After the Battle of Gaixia (202 BC), Liu Bang is proclaimed emperor (Emperor Gaozu, 202–195 BC). Western Han: 202 BC – 9 AD; Eastern Han: 25–220 AD.

events.title: Reign of Emperor Wu of Han
events.descr: The seventh emperor of the Han dynasty, from 141 until his death in 87 BC; his reign lasts 54 years. In 104 BC a new calendar is put into effect.

events.title: Zhang Qian sent to the Western Regions
events.descr: Emperor Wu dispatches his envoy Zhang Qian into the Western Regions.

events.title: Sima Qian’s Shiji
events.descr: Sima Qian (c. 145 – c. 86 BC), historian of the early Han, completes it before 91 BC, probably around 94 BC. In 99 BC he offends Emperor Wu in the Li Ling affair; released from prison in 96 BC, he lives on as a palace eunuch.

sources.sourceLocation: lead and As Han court official

source.sourceLocation: As Han court official (probably around 94 BC)

events.title: The Xin dynasty interrupts the Han
events.descr: Between the Western Han (202 BC – 9 AD) and the Eastern Han (25–220 AD).

events.title: Cai Lun improves papermaking
events.descr: A eunuch official at the court in Luoyang, he substantially improves the papermaking process; earlier forms of paper have existed since the 3rd century BCE.

events.title: Yellow Turban Rebellion
events.descr: It breaks out in March 184, during the reign of Emperor Ling. The main rebellion is suppressed by 185, but subduing the resisting areas takes until 205.

events.title: Battle of Red Cliffs
events.descr: A battle on the Yangtze River in the winter of 208–209. Cao Cao’s southern campaign had started in the autumn of 208.

events.title: End of the Han: the Three Kingdoms
events.descr: The Han abdicates to Cao Wei. The Three Kingdoms period runs from the establishment of Cao Wei in 220 to the conquest of Wu by Jin in 280; other starts proposed include 184, 189, 190 and 196.

events.title: Jin reunites China
events.descr: The Western Jin, established in 266 as successor to Cao Wei, conquers Eastern Wu, ending the Three Kingdoms period. Shu Han had fallen to Wei in 263.

events.title: War of the Eight Princes
events.descr: A series of civil wars; in 304 the dynasty faces a wave of rebellions, the start of the Sixteen Kingdoms.

events.title: Luoyang sacked; the Jin move south
events.descr: Luoyang is sacked in 311 and Chang’an captured in 316, ending the Western Jin (266–316). In 317 the Eastern Jin begins at Jiankang, south of the Huai River.

events.title: The Eastern Jin defeat the Former Qin
events.descr: A devastating defeat for the Former Qin, which from 376 to 383 had unified all of northern and northwest China and Sichuan.

events.title: Northern Wei unifies the north
events.descr: The unification of northern China ends the Sixteen Kingdoms period. The Northern Wei, established on 20 February 386, rules from Pingcheng until it moves its capital to Luoyang on 25 October 493.

events.title: Sui reunites China
events.descr: Yang Jian takes the throne on 4 March 581; in 588 the Sui mass 518,000 troops along the Yangtze, and by 589 Sui troops enter Jiankang.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox and Foundation and Emperor Wen

events.title: The Grand Canal completed
events.descr: The network is expanded and completed by Emperor Yang of Sui; its oldest sections date to the early 5th century BC.

events.title: The Tang dynasty founded
events.descr: Established on 18 June 618; the Sui is abolished by Li Yuan (Emperor Gaozu of Tang, 618–626). Emperor Yang of Sui had been assassinated by Yuwen Huaji in 618.

events.title: Xuanwu Gate Incident
events.descr: A palace coup for the Tang throne on 2 July 626. Within three days Li Shimin is crown prince; about two months later Emperor Gaozu abdicates in his favour (Emperor Taizong, 626–649).

events.title: Wiman seizes Gojoseon
events.descr: The ruling dynasty of Old Chosŏn is overthrown by Wiman. Tradition places the founding by Tan’gun in 2333 BCE, a date the page calls mythological.

events.title: Han conquers Gojoseon
events.descr: The Han dynasty under Emperor Wu invades and conquers Wiman Joseon in the Gojoseon–Han War and establishes commanderies in its place (Lelang, 108 BCE – 313 CE; Xuantu from 107 BCE).

events.title: Goguryeo annexes Lelang
events.descr: Lelang had been ruled by the Jin dynasty until 313. Daifang falls in 314–315 and Xuantu in 319.

events.title: Goguryeo adopts Buddhism
events.descr: The first of the Korean kingdoms to do so; Baekje accepts Buddhism in 384, and Silla adopts it in 527–528.

events.title: Campaigns of Gwanggaeto the Great
events.descr: Goguryeo’s capital moves from Gungnae to Pyongyang in 427.

events.title: Baekje loses the Seoul region
events.descr: The Seoul region falls to Goguryeo; Baekje’s capital is at Ungjin (Gongju) from 475 to 538, when King Seong moves it to Sabi.

events.title: Silla adopts Buddhism
events.descr: Buddhism becomes Silla’s state and official religion from 527.

events.title: Goguryeo–Sui War
events.descr: Sui’s campaigns end in defeat by 614.

events.title: Goguryeo–Tang War
events.descr: Silla, allied with Tang China, conquers Baekje in 660 and Goguryeo in 668 (the fall of Pyongyang).

events.title: The Yamato kingship begins
events.descr: Usually believed to have begun c. 250. Kofun tombs are built for the ruling class from the 3rd to the 7th centuries.

events.title: Buddhism reaches Japan
events.descr: According to the Nihon Shoki (720), Buddhism and the Chinese characters are introduced from Baekje; the date marks the end of the Kofun period and the start of the Asuka period.

events.title: Seventeen-article constitution
events.descr: According to the Nihon Shoki of 720, a document authored by Prince Shōtoku, adopted in the reign of Empress Suiko (r. 593–628).

events.title: Isshi incident and the Taika Reform
events.descr: A palace coup on 10 July 645 (the Isshi incident) is followed by the Taika Reform; the era of 645–649 is named Taika.

events.title: Modu Chanyu founds the Xiongnu Empire
events.descr: Modu kills his father Touman in 209 BCE and rules until 174 BCE. By 208 BCE the Donghu are defeated (they splinter into the Xianbei and Wuhuan), and in 203 BCE he defeats the Yuezhi.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead and Rise of the Xiongnu Empire

events.title: Battle of Baideng
events.descr: A Han dynasty vanguard, in an army led by Emperor Gaozu, is encircled at Mount Baideng near Pingcheng for seven days. In 198 BC a marriage alliance (heqin) is concluded between the Han and the Xiongnu.

events.title: The Xiongnu defeat the Yuezhi
events.descr: After a major defeat, the Yuezhi split into two groups; the majority begin migrating west to the Ili valley in 165 BCE.

events.title: The Great Yuezhi settle in Bactria
events.descr: The Wusun, allied with the Xiongnu, drive the Great Yuezhi out of the Ili valley; they migrate west, then south, and settle in north-west Bactria, where the Han envoy Zhang Qian reaches them in 128 BCE. Around 30 CE one of their tribes, the Kushana, forms the basis of the Kushan Empire.

sources.sourceLocation: timeline table and Exodus of the Great Yuezhi
lead and Migration to the Ili Valley

events.title: Han–Xiongnu wars
events.descr: The tension fully escalates in 133 BC; between 127 and 119 BC Han campaigns push into Mongolia, with a decisive campaign in 119 BC, and a regional protectorate is set up in 60 BC. Some date the conflicts as early as 200 BC and as late as 188 AD.

events.title: The Xiongnu split in two
events.descr: After repeated natural disasters from 46 AD severely weaken the Xiongnu, they permanently split into two groups.

events.title: Defeat of the Northern Xiongnu
events.descr: In 89 AD Dou Xian leads 50,000 cavalry against them; in 91 AD the Northern Chanyu is defeated in the Battle of the Altai Mountains, and the Xianbei begin occupying the Mongolian Plateau, absorbing 100,000 Xiongnu tribes.

events.title: Tanshihuai unifies the Xianbei
events.descr: He unifies the Xianbei in the mid-2nd century and raids the Han dynasty’s northern borders, first in 156; after his death in 181 the Xianbei splinter.

events.title: Bumin overthrows the Rouran: the Turkic Khaganate
events.descr: In 552 Bumin defeats Anagui north of Huaihuang, effectively ending the Rouran, which had dominated the eastern steppe for a century and a half; Muqan Qaghan finishes off the remaining Rouran, who resist until 555.

events.title: Turkic and Byzantine embassies
events.descr: First contact is believed to have happened in 563; a Turkic embassy arrives in 568, and in 569 an embassy led by Zemarchus follows.

sources.sourceLocation: History > Relations with the Byzantine Empire

events.title: The Turkic Khaganate splits
events.descr: A civil war follows Taspar Qaghan’s death in 581, the year the Sui dynasty is founded. Tardu briefly reunifies the empire (599–603); after him it splits again in 603 into Eastern and Western khaganates.

events.title: Tang conquers the Eastern Turks
events.descr: Illig Qaghan, the last independent ruler, who had reached the gates of Chang’an in 626, is captured. Tang conquers the Western Turkic Khaganate in 657.

events.title: Kidarite kingdom in Bactria
events.descr: A Kidarite kingdom replaces the Kushano-Sasanians in Bactria; by 365 Kidara I puts his name on the coinage as Kushanshah. Circa 390–410 the Kidarites invade north-western India.

events.title: The Hephthalites defeat the Kidarites
events.descr: From 450 the Hephthalites are militarily important; by 479 they have conquered Sogdia and driven the Kidarites eastwards, and by 493 they hold parts of Dzungaria and the Tarim Basin.

events.title: Turks and Sasanians destroy the Hephthalites
events.descr: In 557 Istämi allies with Khosrow I of the Sasanian Empire; their combined forces defeat the Hephthalites in 560, who then survive as principalities in Tokharistan until 710.

events.title: The Alans appear in the Caucasus
events.descr: Between 50 and 60 CE the Alans appear in the foothills of the Caucasus. In the 3rd century the Goths break Sarmatian dominance of the Pontic Steppe.

sources.sourceLocation: lead and In the Pontic Steppe and Europe

events.title: The Huns reach the Volga
events.descr: By 370 the Huns have arrived on the Volga, causing the westward movement of Goths and Alans; in 376 the Goths cross the Danube. By 430 the Huns have a vast but short-lived empire on the Danubian frontier.

events.title: Attila rules the Huns
events.descr: He rules jointly with his brother Bleda until Bleda’s death in 445; in 441 he invades the Eastern Roman Empire. He dies in early 453.

events.title: Battle of the Catalaunian Plains
events.descr: On 20 June 451, after Attila crosses the Rhine and invades Gaul, Aetius and Theodoric (who is killed) meet him in battle; the result is inconclusive. In 452 the Huns invade Italy.

events.title: Battle of Nedao: the Hunnic empire breaks up
events.descr: After Attila’s death in 453 the Huns lose much of their empire. Attila’s son Dengizich dies in 469.

events.title: The Avar Khaganate
events.descr: The Pannonian Avars enter the historical scene in the mid-6th century; their khaganate is established in 567 and lasts until 822.

events.title: Avar–Byzantine wars
events.descr: The wars run from 568 to 626, the year the Avars are defeated by Samo.

events.title: Masinissa’s kingdom of Numidia
events.descr: During the Second Punic War Masinissa, king of the Massylii, defeats Syphax of the Masaesyli; with Scipio he beats Syphax and Hasdrubal at Cirta in 203 BC. After Zama (202 BC) he rules Numidia until his death in 148 BC, aged about 90, and by 158 BC has conquered Lepcis Magna and the Tripolitanian coast.

events.title: Masinissa’s war with Carthage
events.descr: Masinissa seizes more Carthaginian territory in 152 BC; Carthage invades his lands in 151 BC with 52,000 men, breaking the peace treaty of 201 BC, and its general Hasdrubal is decisively defeated by Masinissa’s son Gulussa in 150 BC. In 146 BC Carthage is obliterated.

events.title: Jugurthine War
events.descr: In 113 BC Jugurtha again declares war on his cousin; Rome declares war on him in 111 BC, and Metellus arrives in Africa in 109 BC. Mauretania fights on Jugurtha’s side from 107 BC and on Rome’s in 105 BC.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead and Jugurtha and Numidia

events.title: Numidia becomes a Roman province
events.descr: Juba I’s reign (60–46 BC) ends. The Numidia infobox dates the annexation by the Roman Empire to 25 BC.

events.title: Juba II: Mauretania a Roman client kingdom
events.descr: After Bocchus II bequeaths his kingdom to Octavian (33 BC), Augustus makes Mauretania a client kingdom in 25 BC under Juba II, who marries Cleopatra Selene II the same year. In AD 21 Juba makes his son Ptolemy co-ruler.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, infobox, History and monarch table

events.title: Rome annexes Mauretania
events.descr: Caligula orders the execution of King Ptolemy in 40 AD; after Aedemon’s death in 42 AD, Sabalus surrenders in 44 AD and the region is annexed to Rome.

events.title: Balbus campaigns against the Garamantes
events.descr: The Romans capture fifteen Garamantian settlements. The earliest written record of the Garamantes, by Herodotus, dates to the 5th century BC.

events.title: Septimius Severus captures Garama
events.descr: The Garamantian capital falls to Rome. The Garamantes first emerge as a major regional power in the mid-2nd century AD and flourish until the late 7th century.

events.title: The Vandals cross into Africa
events.descr: An estimated 80,000 Vandals under Gaiseric cross from Hispania in 429. They besiege Hippo Regius in 430, where St. Augustine dies on 28 August 430, three months into the siege; peace is made with Rome in 435.

events.title: The Vandals take Carthage
events.descr: Gaiseric breaks the treaty and captures Carthage, which becomes his capital. The Vandals raid Sicily in 440, and peace is secured in 442.

events.title: The Vandals sack Rome
events.descr: In the 460s the Romans launch two expeditions by sea against the Vandal kingdom.

events.title: Belisarius conquers the Vandal kingdom
events.descr: The kingdom ends after 99 years; Gelimer (530–534) is its last ruler.

events.title: Royal burials move to Meroë: the Meroitic period
events.descr: Under Arakamani the royal burial ground moves from Napata to Meroë, and Napata loses its symbolic role. The pyramids of Meroë are built from c. 300 BC to about 350 AD.

events.title: The Meroitic script
events.descr: Developed at the beginning of the Meroitic period to write the Meroitic language; the cursive form predates the earliest surviving hieroglyphic inscription by a century or more. It was deciphered by Francis Llewellyn Griffith (1909, or 1911 in the body of the page).

source.sourceLocation: footnote 2 (Rilly: 'first half of the 3rd Cent. BC')

events.title: Kush at war with Rome; peace with Amanirenas
events.descr: After a Nubian attack on southern Egypt, the Roman governor Petronius invades Nubia and sacks Napata (22 BC; 23 BC on the Napata page). A peace treaty is signed in 22 BC between Rome and Meroë under Augustus and Amanirenas.

events.title: Nero’s expedition reaches Meroë
events.descr: In the autumn of 61 AD a Praetorian party sent by Nero reaches Meroë and goes up the White Nile to the Sudd. The kingdom begins to fade as a power by the 1st or 2nd century AD.

events.title: Aksum takes Meroë: the end of Kush
events.descr: Meroë is already in decline around 300. Aksumites capture Meroë and loot its gold, and Ezana takes the title “King of Ethiopia”; the Aksumite presence is short-lived, and Kush dissolves into Nobatia, Makuria and Alodia.

source.sourceLocation: Fourth Meroitic Period ('In 350 AD Meroë was destroyed by Axum')

events.title: Silko of Nobatia drives out the Blemmyes
events.descr: The first known king of Nobatia claims to have driven the Blemmyes into the Eastern Desert; the capital is set at Pachoras (Faras). The last known Meroitic inscription, of the Blemmye king Kharamadoye at Kalabsha, dates to AD 410/450.

events.title: Dongola founded
events.descr: The Makurian capital; a new Makurian state has emerged by the 5th century, after the collapse of Kush.

events.title: The temple at Philae is closed
events.descr: In the 530s the Byzantines under Justinian pursue a policy of expansion into Nubia.

events.title: The Nubian kingdoms convert to Christianity
events.descr: Nobatia converts in 543; Makuria has “received the faith of Christ” by around 568 and sends a delegation to Constantinople in 573. Alodia, first mentioned in 569, is the last: its request is granted in 580 and Longinus is sent.

events.title: Makuria annexes Nobatia
events.descr: Presumably during the 620s, but before 642; a new bishopric is founded in Faras around 630. The Nobatia page says only that the merger most likely came before 652, and certainly by 707.

events.title: Arab invasions of Makuria and the Baqt
events.descr: A first expedition comes in 641 or 642; a second, under Abd Allah ibn Sa’d ibn Abi al-Sarh, besieges Dongola in 651/652 and is repulsed. The resulting treaty with King Qalidurut, the Baqt, sends 360 slaves a year to Egypt and remains in force for more than six centuries. Alodia is explicitly not affected by it.

events.title: The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea
events.descr: A Greek merchants’ guide to the Red Sea and Indian Ocean; a mid-first-century date is now most commonly accepted. It describes the city of the Auxumites, its ivory trade, and its ruler Zoscales.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Date and authorship, and Aksum section

events.title: Aksum begins minting coins
events.descr: Under King Endybis. Coins are known from eighteen Aksumite kings, from c. 295 until c. 620.

events.title: Reign of Ezana
events.descr: The first Aksumite king to embrace Christianity; his coins replace the pagan disc and crescent with a cross. In about 356 Constantius II writes to him and his brother Saizana.

events.title: Aksum becomes Christian
events.descr: Ezana converts; Frumentius, who came to Aksum as a child around 316, is consecrated its bishop. The coin weights suggest a conversion before Constantine’s reform of 324, or a few years after.

source.sourceLocation: Biography ('or according to others, between 340 and 346')

events.title: The great stelae of Axum
events.descr: The Obelisk of Axum is probably carved and erected during the 4th century AD; the last stele raised in Axum is probably King Ezana’s Stele.

events.title: Reign of Kaleb; Aksum invades Yemen
events.descr: Kaleb invades Yemen around 520 (518–525 in the Aksum infobox), and Aksumite control of West Yemen lasts until c. 525, when Abraha deposes Sumyafa Ashwa. The envoy Nonnosus meets him in 530.

events.title: Aksumite–Persian wars
events.descr: The Aksum infobox lists the Year of the Elephant in 570 and the Aksumite–Persian wars from 570 to 578.

events.title: Muslims take refuge in Aksum
events.descr: The first Hijrah: a small group of early Muslims, then a second of 83 men and 18 women, find refuge with an Aksumite king identified with Armah. They return to Mecca in 622; a second wave goes to Medina in 628.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, The migration(s) and End of the Muslim exile

events.title: Djenné-Djenno settled
events.descr: People first settle the site permanently around 250 BCE (Phase I runs to 50 CE); glass beads there date to as early as the third century BC. A similar settlement at Dia exists from around 900 BCE.

events.title: Eastern Bantu iron-working
events.descr: By the first century BC the Eastern Stream has developed iron forging; from 100 BC to 300 AD it spreads to sites such as Misasa in Tanzania and Kwale in Kenya.

events.title: The Bantu expansion reaches South Africa
events.descr: Bantu speakers reach KwaZulu-Natal by 300 AD and Limpopo Province by 500 AD.

events.title: Djenné-Djenno grows
events.descr: The town covers as much as 100,000 square meters by 400 CE; Phase III runs from about 400 to 900 AD.

events.title: The Arab conquest of Egypt
events.descr: Amr ibn al-As invades in December 639 with some 4,000 men. The Rashidun army wins at Heliopolis on 6 July 640, takes the Babylon Fortress after a siege from September 640 to 6 April 641, and besieges Alexandria from March 641; by September 642 the caliphate has annexed Egypt, Cyrenaica and Tripolitania.

events.title: Celts invade Greece
events.descr: Brennus invades Greece in 281 BC. The La Tène page says Delphi was attacked and sacked in 279 BC; the Galatians page says he was turned back before he could plunder it. Celtic expansion is at its maximum by 275 BC.

events.title: The Galatians settle in Anatolia
events.descr: Celtic settlers come through Thrace under Leogarios and Leonnorios and appear in Asia Minor in 278–277 BC, hired by Nicomedes I of Bithynia. Attalus I of Pergamon defeats them heavily in 240 or 230 BC. Galatia becomes a Roman client state in 64 BC and a province in 25 BC.

events.title: Manlius Vulso’s Galatian War
events.descr: Rome sends Gnaeus Manlius Vulso on an expedition against the Galatians.

events.title: Numantine War
events.descr: A revolt of the Celtiberians of Numantia in Hispania; the first phase ends in 151, and war flares up again in 143. In 134 BC Scipio Aemilianus is sent to end it, and Numantia falls in 133, opening an era of peace in Hispania until the Sertorian War.

events.title: Rome conquers southern Gaul
events.descr: Rome conquers a group of southern Gauls and establishes the province of Transalpine Gaul.

events.title: Cimbrian War
events.descr: Having left the North Sea around 120–115 BC, the Cimbri reach Noricum on the Danube in 113 BC. They invade Gallia Narbonensis in 109 and meet the consul Mallius Maximus and proconsul Caepio at Arausio in 105; Marius is consul five years in a row from 104 BC.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Migrations, Initial defeats, Arausio and Marius

events.title: Caesar’s Gallic Wars
events.descr: Beginning with the migration of the Helvetii in 58 BC, Caesar resolves to conquer all of Gaul (57), defeats the Veneti at sea (56) and crosses to Britain (55–54). Vercingetorix leads a major revolt in 52. The coming civil war withdraws Caesar’s troops in 50; Gaul becomes a Roman province in 27 BC, but resistance lasts until as late as 70 AD.

events.title: Siege of Alesia
events.descr: In September 52 BC Caesar besieges Vercingetorix, building some 25 miles of fortifications in a month; Vercingetorix surrenders.

events.title: Claudius invades Britain
events.descr: Four legions under Aulus Plautius invade; by 47 AD the Romans hold the lands southeast of the Fosse Way. Caligula had massed 200,000 men at the Channel in 40 AD.

events.title: Boudica’s revolt
events.descr: While the governor Suetonius Paulinus campaigns against Mona, Boudica, queen of the Iceni, leads a revolt; Verulamium burns around 60 AD.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Initial actions and Verulamium

events.title: Mons Graupius
events.descr: In mid-84 AD Agricola, governor from 77 AD, faces the Caledonians under Calgacus, concluding the forty-year conquest of Britain.

events.title: Hadrian’s Wall
events.descr: Begun in AD 122, in the reign of Hadrian; most of it takes six years to build, by some 15,000 soldiers of three legions. The turf Antonine Wall follows in AD 142.

events.title: The end of Roman rule in Britain
events.descr: The final Roman withdrawal comes around 410 AD; the Anglo-Saxon settlement page gives the traditional end as 411, and the Chronica Gallica of 452 says Britain was ravaged by Saxon invaders in 409 or 410.

events.title: Britain “handed over” to the Saxons
events.descr: The Chronica Gallica of 452 reports for the year 441 that the British provinces have been handed over across a wide area. Gildas, who probably wrote in the early 6th century, is the main British source.

events.title: Augustine’s mission lands in Kent
events.descr: Sent by Pope Gregory the Great in 596, forty missionaries arrive in 597; King Æthelberht converts before 601, and by 627 Paulinus has converted King Edwin.

events.title: Battle of the Teutoburg Forest
events.descr: Between 8 and 11 September 9 AD, possibly near Kalkriese; the infobox counts 16,000–20,000 killed. The next major Roman incursion into Germania comes under Marcus Aurelius (r. 161–180).

events.title: Marcomannic Wars
events.descr: After incursions into Raetia and Germania Superior (162–165), thousands of Langobardi and Lacringi cross into Pannonia in late 166, beginning wars that last until 180 under Marcus Aurelius.

events.title: Trajan’s Dacian Wars
events.descr: Trajan ends Domitian’s treaty of 89 AD with Decebalus. The first war (101–102) ends when Decebalus makes peace; in the second (105–106) the Dacian capital falls and Decebalus kills himself. Southern Dacia is annexed, and Trajan announces 123 days of celebrations.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, First War, Second War and Aftermath

events.title: The Salian Franks settle in Toxandria
events.descr: The first known Frankish tribe to settle with official Roman permission. The Franks are first named during the crisis of the 3rd century; Constantine executes Frankish prisoners at Trier in 306.

events.title: Alaric I, king of the Visigoths
events.descr: The treaty of 382, after Adrianople, is the first foedus on imperial Roman soil. Alaric, king from 395, sacks Athens in 396 and invades Italy in 401 or 402; he dies at Consentia in 411.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, Early life, Eastern phase and Italy

events.title: Vandals, Alans and Suebi cross the Rhine
events.descr: Traditionally on 31 December 406, near Mainz; Kulikowski argues for 31 December 405. The invaders cross into Spain in September or October 409.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Alternative dating and Aftermath

events.title: The Suebi settle in Gallaecia
events.descr: Under Hermeric the Suebi cross into Iberia on 28 September or 12 October 409; in 411 the invaders divide the provinces of Hispania among themselves. Rechiar (from 448) is the first Germanic king to profess Nicene Christianity.

events.title: The Visigoths settle in Aquitaine
events.descr: Honorius rewards his Visigothic federates under King Wallia with land in the Garonne valley; with their capital at Toulouse they remain de facto independent, becoming a sovereign state in 475.

events.title: Aetius and the Huns destroy the Burgundians
events.descr: King Gundahar, settled on the west bank of the Rhine since 411, is killed in about 436; in 443 the remaining Burgundians are resettled in Sapaudia.

events.title: The Visigoths annex the Suebi
events.descr: King Leovigild conquers the Suebic kingdom, after campaigns starting in the 570s.

events.title: The Visigoths renounce Arianism
events.descr: Under Reccared (586–601) Catholic Christianity becomes the official religion of the kingdom. The Visigothic Code is completed in 654.

events.title: The Byzantines are expelled from Spain
events.descr: Swinthila ends Byzantine Spania (552–624); by 625 only a foothold at Ceuta remains.

events.title: Theodoric conquers Italy
events.descr: Ordered by Zeno to overthrow Odoacer, Theodoric sets out in the autumn of 488 and wins at the Isonzo (28 August 489), Verona and the Adda (11 August 490). Ravenna yields by treaty in February 493, and on 15 March Theodoric kills Odoacer at a banquet.

events.title: Reign of Theodoric the Great in Italy
events.descr: King of the Ostrogoths since 471, he rules Italy from Ravenna from 15 March 493 until his death on 30 August 526, and the Visigoths as regent from 511. He visits Rome in 500; Boethius is executed in 524.

events.title: Justinian’s Gothic War
events.descr: The first phase ends with the fall of Ravenna in 540; the second runs from 540/541. In 554 Justinian issues a pragmatic sanction, though some northern cities hold out until 562. The Ostrogothic kingdom ends with Mons Lactarius in 553.

events.title: The Lombards invade Italy
events.descr: In the spring of 568 King Alboin leads the Lombards from Pannonia into Italy. In 572, after Pavia capitulates and becomes the royal capital, Alboin is assassinated.

events.title: Clovis I unites the Franks
events.descr: Clovis succeeds his father Childeric at 15. He defeats Syagrius at Soissons (486) and the Alemanni at Tolbiac (496), and by 509 has united all the Franks and northern Gallo-Romans. He dies on 27 November 511; Salic law is first codified that year.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Background and Middle reign

events.title: Clovis is baptised
events.descr: He converts to Nicene Christianity rather than Arianism.

events.title: Battle of Vouillé
events.descr: Around spring 507, near Poitiers, Clovis defeats and kills Alaric II; the Franks conquer Gallia Aquitania, and the Visigothic capital moves from Toulouse to Barcelona (507–542), then Toledo.

events.title: The Franks conquer Burgundy
events.descr: The Frankish campaign ends near Autun in 534, and Burgundy becomes part of Francia; the Franks extend their rule into Raetia in 537.

events.title: Clotaire II reunites the Frankish realm
events.descr: The realm, divided since Clovis’s death in 511, is reunited under one ruler. Dagobert I, the last powerful Merovingian king, dies in 639.

events.title: Jordanes’s Getica
events.descr: The first written use of the name “Slavs” dates to the 6th century; Jordanes describes them in his Getica of 551.

events.title: The Slavs expand west and south
events.descr: Between the sixth and seventh centuries Slavs come to control large parts of Europe, reaching the Elbe, the Alps and the Balkans; Carantania is established in the 7th century.

source.sourceLocation: lead ('Between the sixth and seventh centuries')
